opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first instinct, especially if you've been programming for a long time, is to assume the system has made a mistake. Sometimes it has. But I've learned to hold that instinct back a little. Some of the most interesting moments we've had, going back to AlphaGo and move 37, were when the system did something that looked wrong to expert eyes and turned out to be deeply right. Code can be like that too.

So my approach is fairly scientific. I treat it as a hypothesis rather than a verdict. Why might it have done it this way? Is there an edge case it's handling that I hadn't considered? Is it optimizing for something different from what I had in mind? Then you test it empirically: run it, probe it with inputs, see where it breaks or doesn't. Often you either find a genuine bug, which is useful feedback, or you find that your own mental model was incomplete, which is even more useful.

What I try not to do is accept it blindly or reject it reflexively. Both are failure modes. These systems are getting very capable, but they can be confidently wrong in subtle ways, so verification is essential. Still, I think the right posture is curiosity. If something surprises you, that's information. It's either telling you something about the model's limitations or something about the problem you hadn't seen. Either way, you learn something, and that's how I like to approach most things in science.

r001.rationale: The response says code that looks wrong may reflect an edge case the evaluator missed or an incomplete mental model, and gives AlphaGo’s apparently wrong but deeply right move as an analogy.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I try to do is resist the instinct to assume I'm right and the system is wrong. That sounds like a small thing, but it's actually quite important, because the whole history of this field, from AlphaGo onwards, has taught us that when a system does something surprising, there are really two possibilities. Either it's made a mistake, or it's seen something you haven't. And in the early days of AlphaGo, we had exactly this experience with move 37, where all the experts in the room thought it was a blunder, and it turned out to be one of the most creative moves in the history of the game. So I carry that humility with me.

Having said that, with code it's a bit different from Go, because Go has a very clean objective. You either win or you lose. Code has a specification that lives partly in your head, and the model may have inferred a slightly different one. So the practical thing I do is I try to separate those two questions. First, is it actually wrong, meaning does it fail to meet the requirement? And second, if it's not wrong, is it just an unfamiliar way of getting there? Very often it's the second, and I've learned something about a different approach, perhaps a more elegant one.

The way you discipline that is through verification rather than intuition. You write the test, you run it, you look at the edge cases. One of the things I find fascinating about code as a domain is that it's quite close to what I'd call a verifiable domain, a bit like mathematics or games. You can check the answer. And that's precisely why I think it's one of the areas where these systems will improve the fastest, because you can set up a loop where the system proposes, something checks, and it learns from that.

But I'd add a cautionary note. When code looks wrong and is wrong, the failure mode is often subtle. It's not a syntax error, it's a confident-looking function that handles ninety-five percent of cases and quietly mishandles the rest. That's where I think the human judgement still matters enormously, at least for now. You have to ask what assumptions the system baked in that I didn't state. It's a kind of scientific method applied to the collaboration itself. Form a hypothesis about what the model thought you wanted, test it, revise.

And honestly, I find that process intellectually enjoyable. It's a little like working with a very fast, very well-read colleague who has slightly different intuitions from you. Sometimes they're wrong, sometimes you're wrong, and the interesting cases are the ones where you both end up somewhere neither of you would have reached alone.

r001.rationale: The response says a surprising system output may reflect something the evaluator has not seen, and applies that idea to code by distinguishing actual errors from unfamiliar approaches that may teach the evaluator something.

astra-6.text: I try to be careful not to equate “that’s not how I would have written it” with “that’s wrong.” The first thing is to understand what the code is actually doing, then test it against the specification. Can I find a counterexample? What happens at the boundaries? If it fails, then we have something concrete to work with. But if it survives those checks, I have to be willing to update my own intuition. It might have found an approach I hadn’t considered. Of course, passing a few tests isn’t proof of correctness, so the level of verification has to match what you’re going to use it for.

r001.rationale: The response says the code may have found an approach the evaluator had not considered and urges them to update their intuition.

sol-6.1.text: I try to treat that initial reaction as a hypothesis. The code might be wrong, but I might also be missing something about the approach it’s taken. So I’d ask it to explain the reasoning, look carefully at the assumptions, and then test it—particularly on edge cases. The interesting thing is when something looks unfamiliar but turns out to be correct. You don’t want your intuition to rule that out. But equally, a convincing explanation isn’t enough. Ultimately, you want evidence that the code does what you intended.

r001.rationale: The response says the code may only seem wrong because the evaluator is missing something about its approach, and notes that an unfamiliar approach can turn out to be correct.
